query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with density below 6 g/cm³, non-equilibrium solid solution regions will preferentially transform into stable intermetallic compounds upon thermal exposure, and this structural evolution will increase corrosion resistance but decrease high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
generation.material_initial_state: Induction-melted, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g., MgAlCuZnGd or AlMgₓTiSnZn) with a mixture of solid solution and metastable phases, density <6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal annealing at elevated temperature (e.g., 400–600°C) for sufficient time to promote phase transformation.
generation.conditions: Ambient atmosphere for corrosion testing; oxidizing atmosphere (air) for high-temperature oxidation testing; density constraint <6 g/cm³; initial state must be non-equilibrium/metastable.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation from metastable solid solution regions to stable intermetallic compounds (e.g., Mg-rich intermetallics, Al–Mg–Zn phases).
generation.mechanism: Thermal exposure drives diffusion and nucleation of intermetallic compounds, reducing compositional heterogeneity. The resulting intermetallics act as corrosion barriers but provide pathways for rapid oxidation at high temperature due to their microstructural connectivity and lower oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: After annealing, the alloy will show improved corrosion resistance (lower corrosion rate) but worsened high-temperature oxidation resistance (higher mass gain or oxide scale growth) compared to the initial non-equilibrium state.
generation.baseline: Corrosion and oxidation rates of the as-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing HEA before annealing.
generation.boundary: Prediction holds for alloys with density <6 g/cm³, initial non-equilibrium microstructure, and sufficient Mg content to promote intermetallic formation; does not apply to fully equilibrium or single-phase alloys.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of change in corrosion and oxidation rates depends on specific alloy composition and annealing parameters; effect may be less pronounced if intermetallics are discontinuous or if protective oxide films form.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples: one as-cast (non-equilibrium), one annealed at 500°C for 24h. Measure corrosion rate in saline solution and high-temperature oxidation rate in air at 600°C for both sets.
measurements: Corrosion rate (e.g., weight loss or electrochemical current)
Oxidation rate (e.g., mass gain, oxide scale thickness)
Microstructural characterization (phase identification before and after annealing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not show both increased corrosion resistance and decreased high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
